title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Sharp exponential-sum bounds

title: Remark
body_md:
Independently, Robles \cite{Robles2026} proved the folklore
conjecture for all $1$-bounded multiplicative functions,
in the wider range $q\leqslant x/(\log x)^2$ under the weaker approximation condition
$|\alpha-a/q|\leqslant q^{-2}$. His result gives the conjectured
upper bound, but does not determine the sharp leading
constants $4/\sqrt6$ and $1$ as in our
Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
head: environment

label: cor:sharp-range
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:sharp-range}
Suppose that $q=o((\log x)^2)$ and that the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} hold. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:subcritical-general}
 |S_f(x,\alpha)|
 \leqslant
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
For completely multiplicative $f$, the constant
$4/\sqrt6$ can be replaced by $1$.
Both constants are optimal, and neither estimate
can be extended uniformly to $q\asymp(\log x)^2$
with the same leading constant.
head: environment

label: cor:logarithmic
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:logarithmic}
Let $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{U}$ be multiplicative, and suppose that
$|\alpha-a/q|\leqslant1/(qx)$, where $(a,q)=1$ and
$1\leqslant q\leqslant x$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:logarithmic-corollary}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}\frac{f(n)}n\mathrm e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \ll \log q+\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
In particular, conjecture~(1.5) of
\cite{GranvilleLamzouri2026} holds.

Moreover, if
$q=o((\log x/\log\log x)^2)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-sharp-log}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}\frac{f(n)}n\mathrm e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \leqslant
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)
 \frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, the stronger
estimate
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-sharp-log}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}\frac{f(n)}n\mathrm e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \leqslant
 (1+o(1))\frac{\log x}{\sqrt q}
\end{equation}
holds in the same range.

The leading constants $4/\sqrt6$ and $1$ are
best possible for multiplicative and completely
multiplicative functions, respectively.
All estimates are uniform in $f,a,q$, and $\alpha$.
head: environment
name: Logarithmic exponential sums

label: prop:counterexamples
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:counterexamples}
The following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}

\item
There are $1$-bounded multiplicative functions $f_j$
and parameters $q_j,x_j\to\infty$, with
$q_j\leqslant(\log x_j)^2$, such that
\[
 |S_{f_j}(x_j,1/q_j)|
 =
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)
 \frac{x_j}{\sqrt{q_j}}.
\]
Thus the leading constant $1$ in conjecture~(1.3)
is false for general multiplicative functions.

\item
There are squarefree integers $q_j\to\infty$,
real numbers $x_j\geqslant y_j\geqslant q_j^2$ tending to
infinity, reduced numerators $a_j$, and periodic
unimodular multiplicative functions $f_j$ such that
\[
 \frac{
 \left|
 \sum_{\substack{n\leqslant x_j\\P^+(n)\leqslant y_j}}
 f_j(n)\mathrm e(a_jn/q_j)
 \right|
 }{
 \Psi(x_j,y_j)/\sqrt{q_j}
 +\sqrt{x_jy_j}/\log x_j
 }
 \longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Hence conjecture~(1.4) fails in order of magnitude.

\item
For $f\equiv1$ and
$q=\lfloor(\log x/\log\log x)^2\rfloor$, we have
\[
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}\frac{\mathrm e(n/q)}n
 \right|
 =(2+o(1))\log\log x.
\]
This exceeds the proposed upper bound with leading
constant $4/\sqrt6$ in conjecture~(1.6).
Thus that conjecture fails at its stated endpoint,
even for completely multiplicative functions.

\end{enumerate}

label: lem:conv
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Define $h$ multiplicatively by the identity of formal Euler factors
\[
 \sum_{k\geqslant0}\frac{f(p^k)}{p^{ks}}
 =\left(\sum_{k\geqslant0}\frac{h(p^k)}{p^{ks}}\right)
  \left(\sum_{k\geqslant0}\frac{F_q(p^k)}{p^{ks}}\right).
\]
If $p\mid q$, the two factors involving $f$ and $F_q$ are identical, whence $h(p^k)=0$ for every $k\geqslant1$. Suppose that $p\nmid q$. Since $F_q(p^k)=f(p)^k$, comparison of the coefficient of $p^{-s}$ gives $h(p)=0$. For $k\geqslant2$, the coefficient identity reads
$f(p^k)=h(p^k)+f(p)h(p^{k-1})+\cdots+f(p)^k$. Using the same identity at level $k-1$ and multiplying it by $f(p)$, all terms except the first cancel, and therefore
$h(p^k)=f(p^k)-f(p)f(p^{k-1})$.

It follows that $|h(p^k)|\leqslant2$, and that every integer in the support of $h$, apart from $1$, is powerful and coprime to $q$. Hence
\[
 \sum_{d\geqslant1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d}
 \leqslant\prod_{p\nmid q}\left(1+2\sum_{k\geqslant2}\frac1{p^k}\right)
 \leqslant\prod_p\left(1+\frac{2}{p(p-1)}\right)<\infty.
\]
More generally, if $0<\delta<1/2$, then
$\sum_{k\geqslant2}p^{-k(1-\delta)}\ll p^{-2(1-\delta)}$, and the corresponding Euler product converges because $2(1-\delta)>1$. This proves both assertions in \eqref{eq:h-sums}.
head: environment

label: prop:reduction
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:conv-sum
title: Proof
body_md:
Expanding the convolution $f=h*F_q$ and changing the order of summation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conv-sum}
 S_f(x,\alpha)=\sum_{\substack{d\leqslant x\\(d,q)=1}}h(d)S_{F_q}(x/d,d\alpha).
\end{equation}
The restriction $(d,q)=1$ follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:conv}.
Since $(d,q)=1$, $ad$ is also coprime to $q$, and
\[
 d\alpha=\frac{ad}{q}+d(\alpha-a/q),
 \qquad |d(\alpha-a/q)|\leqslant\frac{d}{qx}=\frac1{q(x/d)}.
\]
Thus every inner sum in \eqref{eq:conv-sum} has a rational approximation with the same denominator $q$. This is the point of the definition \eqref{eq:Fq}.

We split the $d$-sum at $\sqrt x$. If $d\leqslant\sqrt x$, then
$x/d\geqslant\sqrt x$ and $\log x\leqslant2\log(x/d)$. Consequently
$q\leqslant(\log x)^3\leqslant8(\log(x/d))^3$, so \eqref{eq:local-goal}
applies. Since $\log(x/d)\asymp\log x$ in this range,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{d\leqslant\sqrt x}|h(d)|\left(\frac{x/d}{\log(x/d)}+\frac{x/d}{\sqrt q}\right)
 &\ll \left(\frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}\right)
       \sum_{d\geqslant1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d}\\
 &\ll \frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{align*}
For $d>\sqrt x$ we use $|S_{F_q}(x/d,d\alpha)|\leqslant x/d$.
Taking $\delta=1/4$ in \eqref{eq:h-sums},
\[
 x\sum_{d>\sqrt x}\frac{|h(d)|}{d}
 \leqslant x^{7/8}\sum_{d\geqslant1}\frac{|h(d)|}{d^{3/4}}
 \ll x^{7/8}=o(x/\log x).
\]
Combining the two ranges proves the proposition.
head: environment

label: prop:large-prime
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $n\leqslant x$ satisfy $P^{+}(n)>x/q$. Since $x/q>\sqrt x$, the largest prime factor of $n$ occurs to the first power and is the unique prime factor of $n$ exceeding $x/q$. Thus $n=pm$ uniquely, where $p>x/q$ is prime and $m<x/p<q$. In particular $p\nmid m$, so ordinary multiplicativity gives $F(pm)=F(p)F(m)$.

For $1\leqslant k<q$, put $I_k=(x/(k+1),x/k]$ and
$A_k(b):=\sum_{m\leqslant k}F(m)\mathrm e(abm/q)$. The condition $p\in I_k$ is equivalent to $\lfloor x/p\rfloor=k$, and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-prime-decomp}
 \sum_{\substack{n\leqslant x\\P^{+}(n)>x/q}}F(n)\mathrm e(an/q)
 =\sum_{k<q}\sum_{p\in I_k}F(p)A_k(p).
\end{equation}
The length of $I_k$ is
$|I_k|=x/(k(k+1))\asymp x/k^2$. Since $k<q\leqslant8L^3$, we have
$|I_k|/q\geqslant x/q^3=x^{1-o(1)}$. The short-interval
Brun--Titchmarsh inequality bounds the primes in an interval of length
$H>q$ and a reduced class by
$\ll H/\{\phi(q)\log(H/q)\}$. Applying this to $I_k$ as in
\cite[(3.20)]{GranvilleLamzouri2026} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:BT}
 \#\{p\in I_k:p\equiv b\pmod q\}
 \ll \frac{x}{\phi(q)k^2\log x}
\end{equation}
for every reduced residue class $b\pmod q$, uniformly in $k<q$. Here the logarithm in Brun--Titchmarsh is $\log(|I_k|/q)\asymp\log x$.

Define
$\mathcal E_q(k):=\phi(q)^{-1}\sum_{b\bmod q,(b,q)=1}|A_k(b)|^2$. Grouping the primes in the inner sum of \eqref{eq:large-prime-decomp} by residue class, and then using \eqref{eq:BT}, gives
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{p\in I_k}F(p)A_k(p)\right|
 &\leqslant\sum_{\substack{b\bmod q\\(b,q)=1}}|A_k(b)|
       \#\{p\in I_k:p\equiv b\pmod q\}\\
 &\ll \frac{x}{\phi(q)k^2\log x}
       \sum_{\substack{b\bmod q\\(b,q)=1}}|A_k(b)|\\
 &\leqslant \frac{x}{k^2\log x}\sqrt{\mathcal E_q(k)}.
\end{align*}
Thus each $k$-block is bounded by $x\sqrt{\mathcal E_q(k)}/(k^2\log x)$.

We estimate $\mathcal E_q(k)$ in two different ways. Enlarging the average from the reduced residue classes to all additive frequencies and applying Parseval gives
\[
 \mathcal E_q(k)
 \leqslant\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{b\bmod q}|A_k(b)|^2
 =\frac q{\phi(q)}\sum_{m\leqslant k}|F(m)|^2
 \leqslant\frac q{\phi(q)}k.
\]
For small $k$ one can do better. Expanding the square over reduced residue classes yields the exact identity
\[
 \mathcal E_q(k)=\frac1{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{m,n\leqslant k}F(m)\overline{F(n)}c_q(m-n).
\]
The diagonal contributes at most $k$, while for each $1\leqslant h<k$ there are at most $k$ pairs with $m-n=h$ and at most $k$ with $n-m=h$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:energy-ramanujan}
 \mathcal E_q(k)\leqslant k+2k\sum_{1\leqslant h<k}\frac{|c_q(h)|}{\phi(q)}.
\end{equation}
The prime-power formula for Ramanujan sums implies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ram-support}
 \frac{|c_q(h)|}{\phi(q)}=
 \begin{cases}
  \phi((u,\operatorname{rad}(q)))/\phi(\operatorname{rad}(q)),&h=\frac{q}{\operatorname{rad}(q)}u,\\
  0,&\frac{q}{\operatorname{rad}(q)}\nmid h.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Indeed, for $p^a\Vert q$ the local factor vanishes unless $p^{a-1}\mid h$; after writing $h=(q/\operatorname{rad}(q))u$, it is $1$ if $p\mid u$ and $1/(p-1)$ otherwise. Therefore,
\[
 \sum_{1\leqslant h<k}\frac{|c_q(h)|}{\phi(q)}
 \leqslant\frac1{\phi(\operatorname{rad}(q))}\sum_{u\leqslant k\operatorname{rad}(q)/q}\phi((u,\operatorname{rad}(q)))
 \leqslant\frac{k^2}{\phi(\operatorname{rad}(q))}.
\]
If $k\leqslant(q/\phi(q))^2$, then
\[
 \frac{k^2}{\phi(\operatorname{rad}(q))}\leqslant\frac{(q/\phi(q))^4}{\phi(\operatorname{rad}(q))}
 =\prod_{p\mid q}\frac{p^4}{(p-1)^5}\leqslant\frac{81}{2}.
\]
The last inequality holds because each local factor is less than $1$ for $p\geqslant5$, while the factors at $2$ and $3$ have product $81/2$. Substitution in \eqref{eq:energy-ramanujan} gives
$\mathcal E_q(k)\leqslant82k$ for $k\leqslant(q/\phi(q))^2$.

We now sum the blocks. For $k\leqslant(q/\phi(q))^2$ use the short estimate, and for larger $k$ use Parseval:
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{k<q}\frac{\sqrt{\mathcal E_q(k)}}{k^2}
 &\ll\sum_{k\leqslant(q/\phi(q))^2}k^{-3/2}
   +\sqrt{q/\phi(q)}\sum_{k>(q/\phi(q))^2}k^{-3/2}\\
 &\ll1.
\end{align*}
Summing the preceding block estimate over $k<q$ proves \eqref{eq:large-prime}.

label: lem:shiu-weight
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Shiu's Brun--Titchmarsh theorem for non-negative multiplicative
functions \cite{Shiu1980}, combined with Mertens' estimate, gives
\[
 \sum_{m\leqslant u}w_z(m)
 \ll\frac{u}{\log(2u)}
   \exp\left(\sum_{p\leqslant u}\frac{w_z(p)}p\right)
 \ll u\rho_z(u).
\]
For small $u\ll T$ the same assertion follows trivially, since
$w_z(m)\leqslant1$ and $\rho_z(u)\asymp1$.
For the progression estimate, let $d=(b,q)$, $q_1=q/d$ and $u_1=u/d$.
Dividing the congruence by $d$ gives a reduced class modulo $q_1$.
Every prime dividing $d$ is below $T$, so $w_z(dm)=w_z(m)$.
Moreover $u\geqslant q^4$ ensures $q_1\leqslant u_1^{1/4}$.
Shiu's theorem, with the prime factors of $q_1$ omitted from its
Euler product, gives
\[
 \sum_{\substack{m\leqslant u_1\\m\equiv b/d\pmod{q_1}}}w_z(m)
 \ll\frac{u_1}{\phi(q_1)}\rho_z(u_1)
       \prod_{p\mid q_1}\left(1-\frac1p\right).
\]
Here $w_z(p)=1$ for $p\mid q_1$; the final product cancels
$q_1/\phi(q_1)$. Since $d\leqslant q\leqslant u^{1/4}$,
$\rho_z(u/d)\ll\rho_z(u)$ uniformly in $z$.
We obtain $u_1\rho_z(u_1)/q_1\ll u\rho_z(u)/q$.

label: lem:ramare-mass
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $t_{j+1}/t_j=1+O(t_j^{-1/3})$, the left-hand side is
bounded by a constant times
\[
 x\int_0^1\int_T^{2y}\frac{\rho_z(x/t)}{t\log t}\,\mathrm{d} t\,\mathrm{d} z.
\]
For $u>T$, integration in $z$ gives
\[
 \int_0^1\rho_z(u)\,\mathrm{d} z
 \leqslant\min\left\{1,
   \frac1{\log\{\log(2u)/\log(2T)\}}\right\}
\]
whenever the second expression is defined with positive denominator.
For $T\leqslant t\leqslant\sqrt x$ we have $u=x/t\geqslant\sqrt x$;
the $z$-integral is $O(1/\log L)$, while
$\int_T^{\sqrt x}\mathrm{d} t/(t\log t)\ll\log L$.
For $\sqrt x\leqslant t\leqslant2y$ we use $\rho_z\leqslant1$ and
$\int_{\sqrt x}^{2y}\mathrm{d} t/(t\log t)=O(1)$.
Together these estimates prove \eqref{eq:ramare-mass}.

label: lem:gauss-pointwise
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Chinese remainder theorem, it is enough to consider $q=p^a$.
If the local character has conductor $p^b$, $1\leqslant b\leqslant a$,
then $G_{p^a}(v,\chi)$ vanishes unless $v_p(v)=a-b$;
in the nonzero case its modulus equals
$p^{a-b}p^{b/2}=p^{a-b/2}$.
For the principal character the sum is $c_{p^a}(v)$, whose
prime-power formula gives the same pointwise bound.
head: environment

label: lem:gauss-l1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The sum factors over prime powers. For a local conductor $p^b$,
$1\leqslant b\leqslant a$, precisely $\phi(p^b)$ classes have nonzero
Gauss sum, each of modulus $p^{a-b/2}$.
The local $\ell^1$ sum is thus $\phi(p^a)p^{b/2}$,
which is at most $\phi(p^a)p^{a/2}$.
For the principal character the Ramanujan-sum formula gives local
norm $2\phi(p^a)$; relative to $\phi(p^a)p^{a/2}$ it has factor
$2/p^{a/2}$. Only $p^a=2,3$ enlarge the product, and their
factors are $2/\sqrt2$ and $2/\sqrt3$.

title: Proof

label: lem:PLS
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Granville--Harper--Soundararajan

label: prop:weighted-pls
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Every $m$ has a unique factorization $m=dn$ with
$d\in\mathcal D_q$ and $(n,q)=1$. Since $q<T$, we have
$w_z(dn)=w_z(n)$. Define
\[
 g_z(n):=F(n)w_z(n)\mathbf1_{(n,q)=1}.
\]
It is multiplicative and belongs to $\mathcal C(1)$: for $p\nmid q$
and $p>T$ its local generating function equals
\[
 1+z\sum_{k\geqslant1}\frac{F(p)^k}{p^{ks}}
 =\frac{1-(1-z)F(p)p^{-s}}{1-F(p)p^{-s}},
\]
so that
$\Lambda_{g_z}(p^k)=F(p)^k\{1-(1-z)^k\}\log p$;
for $p\leqslant T$ (away from $q$) the usual bound holds, and for
$p\mid q$ the function is zero. Thus $|\Lambda_{g_z}(n)|\leqslant\Lambda(n)$.

For $(n,q)=1$, the change of variables in the Gauss sum gives
$G_q(adn,\overline\chi)=\chi(n)G_q(ad,\overline\chi)$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bj-factor}
 B_{j,z}(\chi)=\sum_{\substack{d\leqslant M_j\\d\in\mathcal D_q}}
 F(d)G_q(ad,\overline\chi)
 \sum_{n\leqslant M_j/d}g_z(n)\chi(n).
\end{equation}
Choose $\chi_{j,z}$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:PLS} with $M=M_j$.
For $d\leqslant\sqrt{M_j}$, Minkowski's inequality, the pointwise
Gauss bound, and the large sieve give the contribution
\[
 \ll\sqrt q\,M_j\mathfrak D(M_j,q)
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}\frac{\sqrt{(d,q)}}d
 \leqslant H(q)\sqrt q\,M_j\mathfrak D(M_j,q).
\]
For $d>\sqrt{M_j}$, use the trivial inner-sum bound $M_j/d$.
Minkowski's inequality and \eqref{eq:gauss-l2} give
\[
 \ll\phi(q)M_j
 \sum_{\substack{d>\sqrt{M_j}\\d\in\mathcal D_q}}\frac1d
 \leqslant H(q)\phi(q)M_j^{3/4}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:weighted-pls}.

label: lem:short-M
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Multiplicative Parseval and the enlargement to all additive
frequencies give
\[
 \sum_\chi|B_{j,z}(\chi)|^2
 \leqslant\phi(q)q\sum_{b\bmod q}
 \left|\sum_{\substack{m\leqslant M_j\\m\equiv b\pmod q}}
                   F(m)w_z(m)\right|^2.
\]
Each residue class contains at most $M_j/q+1$ integers;
$|F(m)w_z(m)|\leqslant1$ and $M_j\geqslant q$, so the last sum is at
most $2\phi(q)M_j^2$.

title: Proposition

label: eq:local-finished
title: Proof
body_md:
We first establish the local statement required in
Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction}. Moduli below a fixed absolute constant are
covered by $|S_F(x,\alpha)|\leqslant x\ll x/\sqrt q$, so we may assume that
$q$ is sufficiently large for the quoted smooth-number estimates. For
$q\leqslant8L^3$, split
$S_F(x,a/q)$ according as $P^{+}(n)$ is at most or greater than $x/q$. Proposition~\ref{prop:large-prime} and Proposition~\ref{prop:smooth-core} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-finished}
 S_F(x,a/q)\ll \frac{x}{\log x}+\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
Lemma~\ref{lem:phase} extends this to $|\alpha-a/q|\leqslant1/(qx)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:reduction} then proves the same estimate for every multiplicative $f$ in the range $q\leqslant(\log x)^3$.

The preceding argument treats $q\leqslant(\log x)^3$. Proposition~\ref{prop:large-q} treats $q\geqslant(\log x)^{5/2}$ up to
$Q_{\rm MV}(x)$. The ranges overlap and exhaust all admissible $q$.

label: lem:general-primary-kernel
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Local Gauss-sum bounds

label: eq:primary-CRT-factor
title: Proof
body_md:
We prove the estimates prime by prime. Factor $q=\prod_{p^e\Vert q}p^e$ and let
$\chi_p$ denote the component of $\chi$ modulo $p^e$.
The Chinese remainder theorem gives a constant $\omega(a,\chi)$ of
modulus one for which
\begin{equation}\label{eq:primary-CRT-factor}
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}\frac{f(d)G_q(ad,\overline\chi)}{d^{1+it}}
 =\omega(a,\chi)
 \prod_{p^e\Vert q}\left(\sum_{v\geqslant0}
  \frac{f(p^v)\chi^{(p)}(p)^v}{p^{v(1+it)}}
  G_{p^e}(p^v,\overline{\chi_p})\right),
\end{equation}
where $\chi^{(p)}=\prod_{\substack{r^b\Vert q\\r\ne p}}\chi_r$;
thus $|\chi^{(p)}(p)|=1$. More explicitly, the CRT expression for
$G_q$ has local additive coefficient $ad(q/p^e)^{-1}$; its unit part
can be removed from the local Gauss sum and contributes precisely the
character factors displayed in \eqref{eq:primary-CRT-factor}.
The factorization also holds after taking absolute values.

For a local character of conductor $p^j$ with $1\leqslant j\leqslant e$,
$G_{p^e}(p^v,\overline{\chi_p})$ vanishes unless $v=e-j$, in which case
its modulus is $p^{e-j/2}$. The corresponding local contribution
to \eqref{eq:general-primary-kernel} is $p^{j/2}\leqslant p^{e/2}$.
For a principal local character the relevant Ramanujan sums are
\[
 c_{p^e}(p^{e-1})=-p^{e-1},\qquad
 c_{p^e}(p^v)=\phi(p^e)\quad(v\geqslant e).
\]
Consequently the local absolute norm equals $2$.
Only the factors $p^e=2,3$ have $2>p^{e/2}$, and their relative
contributions multiply to $4/\sqrt6$.
This proves \eqref{eq:general-primary-kernel}. Replacing $d^{-1}$ by
$d^{-1+\rho}$ gives local norms $p^{j/2+\rho(e-j)}$ in the
nonprincipal case and $O_\rho(p^{\rho e})$ in the principal case.
Their product is $q^{1/2+o(1)}$, proving the weighted bound.

Suppose now that $f$ is completely multiplicative. Set
\[
 z_p=f(p)p^{-it}\chi^{(p)}(p),\qquad |z_p|\leqslant1.
\]
The local factor in \eqref{eq:primary-CRT-factor} is
$\sum_{v\geqslant0}z_p^v p^{-v}G_{p^e}(p^v,\overline{\chi_p})$.
For conductor $p^j$, $j\geqslant1$, this has modulus at most
$p^{j/2}|z_p|^{e-j}\leqslant p^{e/2}$.
For the principal character the complete geometric sum is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:principal-kernel-contraction}
 -z_p^{e-1}+\frac{(1-p^{-1})z_p^e}{1-z_p/p}
 =-z_p^{e-1}\frac{1-z_p}{1-z_p/p}.
\end{equation}
For $|z|\leqslant1$,
\[
 \frac{|1-z|}{|1-z/p|}\leqslant\frac{2p}{p+1}
 \leqslant\sqrt p\leqslant p^{e/2}.
\]
Thus every local factor is at most $p^{e/2}$; multiplying over
$p^e\Vert q$ proves \eqref{eq:complete-primary-kernel}.
The empty product for $q=1$ is understood as $1$.

label: lem:general-level-q-sieve
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:general-powerful-convolution
title: Proof
body_md:
Define a completely multiplicative function $f^\flat$ by
$f^\flat(p)=f(p)$ for $p\nmid q$ and $f^\flat(p)=0$ for $p\mid q$.
There is a multiplicative function $h$, supported on powerful integers
coprime to $q$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-powerful-convolution}
 f(n)\mathbf1_{(n,q)=1}=(h*f^\flat)(n),
 \qquad
 \sum_{n\geqslant1}\frac{|h(n)|}{n^{1-\rho}}\ll_\rho1
 \quad(0<\rho<1/2).
\end{equation}
Indeed, $h(p)=0$ and
$h(p^\nu)=f(p^\nu)-f(p)f(p^{\nu-1})$ for $p\nmid q$ and $\nu\geqslant2$;
the assertion follows from the same Euler-factor calculation as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:conv}.

Apply \cite[Theorem~1.9]{GranvilleHarperSoundararajan2019} with $J=1$
to $f^\flat$, using the base point $x/L^{2A+20}$. Since $q\leqslant L^3$,
the modulus condition is automatic, and the uniform interval in that
theorem contains every $Y/k$ with $x/L^A\leqslant Y\leqslant x$ and
$k\leqslant L^R$, for each fixed $R$. The uniformity in the length gives a set $\mathcal E_q$ of at
most one character for which the analogue of
\eqref{eq:general-level-q-sieve} holds for the means of $f^\flat$,
uniformly throughout the displayed interval.

Expanding \eqref{eq:general-powerful-convolution} and applying Minkowski's
inequality transfers this estimate to $f$. For $k\leqslant L^R$, with $R$
fixed sufficiently large in terms of $A$, the same exceptional character
works at every length $Y/k$, and the total cost is
$\sum |h(k)|/k\ll1$. For $k>L^R$, the trivial character $L^2$ estimate
and \eqref{eq:general-powerful-convolution} give
\[
 \ll \sqrt q\,Y\sum_{k>L^R}\frac{|h(k)|}{k}
 \ll YL^{3/2-R\rho+o(1)}.
\]
Choose $R$ so that this is smaller than the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:general-level-q-sieve}. This proves the lemma.

label: lem:general-weighted-tail
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:weighted-uniform-sieve
title: Proof
body_md:
We give the argument with varying cutoffs because the exceptional set must work uniformly for both $X$ and $Y$. By \eqref{eq:general-powerful-convolution}
and Minkowski's inequality, the Granville--Harper--Soundararajan large
sieve for $f^\flat$ transfers to the means $M_\chi(u)$, with the
same exceptional set at each length. Fix $R=40$ and separate the convolution variables at $k=L^R$.
The tail has the following $\ell^2$-norm over characters:
$\ll \sqrt q\,u\sum_{k>L^R}|h(k)|/k
 \ll uL^{3/2-R/4+o(1)}$, which is negligible for the present
purpose. For $k\leqslant L^R$, apply
\cite[Theorem~1.9]{GranvilleHarperSoundararajan2019} with $J=100$
at geometric base points $U_0,U_0^2,U_0^4,\ldots$, where
$U_0=Z_A/L^{2A+R+2}$. With the enlarged value of $Z_A$ above,
$q\leqslant U_0^{1/4}$; the available uniform length intervals cover
all the required $u/k$. There are $O_A(\log L)$ relevant points,
and their exceptional sets have total size $L^{o(1)}$.
After relaxing the fixed large-sieve exponent,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weighted-uniform-sieve}
 \left(\sum_{\chi\notin\mathcal E}|M_\chi(u)|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \ll_A u\left(\frac{\log(qL)}{\log u}\right)^{4/5}
\end{equation}
for $Z_A/L^{2A}\ll u\leqslant x/Z_A$.
The convolution factor supported on powerful numbers has a power-saving tail,
so it only changes the implied constant.

By ordinary multiplicativity, after removing multiples of $p^2$ with
$p>Z_A$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-weighted-factorization}
 \sum_{n\leqslant Y}f(n)\chi(n)w_X(n)
 =\sum_{Z_A<p\leqslant X/Z_A}(\log p)f(p)\chi(p)
                  M_\chi(Y/p)
 +O\left(\frac{Y\log Z_A}{Z_A}\right).
\end{equation}
The error, summed over all $\chi\pmod q$, is negligible in
\eqref{eq:general-weighted-tail} since $Z_A$ is a sufficiently
large fixed power of $qL$.

Partition the primes into dyadic intervals $D<p\leqslant2D$, and each
such interval into pieces $\mathcal I=(V,V+h]$ of length
$h\asymp D^{2/3}$. Weighted Brun--Titchmarsh gives
$\sum_{p\in\mathcal I,\,p\equiv b\pmod q}\log p\ll h/\phi(q)$.
For $P_\chi(\mathcal I)=\sum_{p\in\mathcal I}(\log p)f(p)\chi(p)$,
character orthogonality and a second application of the same bound yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-prime-second}
 \sum_{\chi\pmod q}|P_\chi(\mathcal I)|^2\ll h^2.
\end{equation}
Freezing $M_\chi(Y/p)$ at $M_\chi(Y/V)$, Cauchy--Schwarz,
\eqref{eq:weighted-uniform-sieve}, and \eqref{eq:sharp-prime-second}
bound the frozen contribution of one piece by
\[
 \ll_A\frac{hY}{D}
 \left(\frac{\log(qL)}{\log(Y/D)}\right)^{4/5}.
\]
There are $O(D/h)$ pieces in a dyadic block. The freezing error
in one piece is at most
$q h(1+Yh/D^2)$ after summing over $\chi$, and hence over the whole dyadic block is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sharp-moving-error}
 \ll q(D+YD^{-1/3}).
\end{equation}
Indeed, the interval between $Y/p$ and $Y/V$ has length
$O(Yh/D^2)$, while the sum of the prime weights in a piece is $O(h)$.

Summing the frozen contributions over dyadic $D$ and dividing by
$L=\log x$, a comparison with the integral of $u^{-4/5}$ gives
\[
 \frac1L\sum_DY
 \left(\frac{\log(qL)}{\log(Y/D)}\right)^{4/5}
 \ll_A Y\left(\frac{\log(qL)}L\right)^{4/5}.
\]
The errors from \eqref{eq:sharp-moving-error}, after summation over
$D$ and division by $L$, are
\[
 \ll\frac{q}{L}\left(\frac X{Z_A}+YZ_A^{-1/3}\right)
 =o\left(Y\left(\frac{\log Z_A}{L}\right)^{2/3}\right).
\]
Because $4/5>2/3$, the required bound follows.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Partition $1\leqslant u\leqslant Z$ into intervals $(u_j,u_{j+1}]$
with $u_{j+1}-u_j\asymp\sqrt{u_j}$, and group primes according
to $X/u_{j+1}<p\leqslant X/u_j$. Put
$V_j(b)=\sum_{m\leqslant u_j}f(m)\mathrm e(abm/q)$.
Replacing the inner cutoff $X/p$ by $u_j$ costs at most
\[
 \ll X\sum_j\frac{(u_{j+1}-u_j)^2}{u_j^2}=O(X).
\]
Weighted Brun--Titchmarsh bounds the contribution of one prime
block by
\[
 \ll\frac{X(u_{j+1}-u_j)}{u_j^2\phi(q)}
         \sum_{(b,q)=1}|V_j(b)|.
\]
By Cauchy--Schwarz and the Ramanujan identity
$c_q(h)=\sum_{d\mid(q,h)}d\mu(q/d)$,
\[
 \left(\sum_{(b,q)=1}|V_j(b)|\right)^2
 \leqslant\phi(q)u_j\sum_{|h|\leqslant u_j}|c_q(h)|,
 \qquad
 \sum_{|h|\leqslant T}|c_q(h)|\ll\phi(q)+T2^{\omega(q)}.
\]
Consequently the sum of the prime blocks is at most
\[
 \ll X\sum_j\frac{u_{j+1}-u_j}{u_j^{3/2}}
     +\frac{X2^{\omega(q)/2}}{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}
           \sum_j\frac{u_{j+1}-u_j}{u_j}
 \ll X+\frac{X2^{\omega(q)/2}}{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}\log(2Z).
\]
Combining with the freezing error proves the lemma.

title: Proposition

name: Reduction to a single character

label: eq:general-logarithmic-identity
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a sufficiently large fixed $R=R(A)$ and write
$B=A+R+1$. Throughout the proof we use the weight in
\eqref{eq:general-prime-weight} with $A$ replaced by $B$; thus its
threshold is $Z_B=(qL^{B+2})^4$. We first estimate the boundary terms. Uniformly for $x/L^A\leqslant X\leqslant x$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-logarithmic-identity}
 (\log X)S_f(X,a/q)
 =\sum_{n\leqslant X}f(n)\mathrm e(an/q)w_X(n)
 +O_A(X)+o\left(\frac{XL}{\sqrt q}\right).
\end{equation}

Indeed,
\[
 \log n-w_X(n)
 =\sum_{\substack{p^j\mid n\\p\leqslant Z_B}}\log p
  +\sum_{\substack{p^j\mid n\\p>X/Z_B}}\log p
  +\sum_{\substack{p^j\mid n,\ j\geqslant2\\Z_B<p\leqslant X/Z_B}}\log p.
\]
The final sum has total mass
$O(X\sum_{p>Z_B}(\log p)/p^2)=O(X/Z_B)$. For the first sum, separate the
exact valuation $p^k\Vert n$. If $p^k\leqslant Z_B^2$, Proposition~\ref{prop:basic-bound}
applied at length $X/p^k$ and reduced denominator $q/(q,p^k)$ gives
\[
 \sum_{\substack{m\leqslant X/p^k\\(m,p)=1}}
 f(m)\mathrm e(ap^km/q)
 \ll_A \frac{X}{p^kL}
       +\frac{X}{p^k\sqrt{q/(q,p^k)}}.
\]
After summing with weight $k\log p$, the first terms contribute
$O_A(X\log Z_B/L)=O_A(X)$, while the second terms are
\[
 \ll \frac{X}{\sqrt q}
 \sum_{p^k\leqslant Z_B^2}
 \frac{k(\log p)\sqrt{(q,p^k)}}{p^k}
 =\frac{X}{\sqrt q}L^{o(1)}\log Z_B
 =o\left(\frac{XL}{\sqrt q}\right).
\]
The terms with $p^k>Z_B^2$ have total mass $O(X\log Z_B/Z_B)$.

For the second sum, $p>X/Z_B$ implies $p^2>X$ for sufficiently large
$x$. Hence its contribution is
\[
 \sum_{p>X/Z_B}f(p)\log p
 \sum_{m\leqslant X/p}f(m)\mathrm e(apm/q).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:weighted-large-prime-boundary}, with $Z=Z_B$,
bounds this by
\[
 O_A(X)+O\left(
  \frac{X2^{\omega(q)/2}}{\sqrt{\phi(q)}}\log(2Z_B)
 \right)
 =O_A(X)+o\left(\frac{XL}{\sqrt q}\right).
\]
Finally, $\sum_{n\leqslant X}\log(X/n)\ll X$. These estimates prove
\eqref{eq:general-logarithmic-identity}.

For a character $\chi\pmod q$, write
\[
 W_{\chi,X}(Y):=\sum_{n\leqslant Y}f(n)\chi(n)w_X(n).
\]
Since every prime dividing $q$ is smaller than $Z_B$, one has
$w_X(dm)=w_X(m)$ whenever $d\in\mathcal D_q$ and $(m,q)=1$. Thus
Fourier inversion gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-weighted-primary}
 \sum_{n\leqslant X}f(n)\mathrm e(an/q)w_X(n)
 =\frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{\chi\bmod q}
   \sum_{\substack{d\leqslant X\\d\in\mathcal D_q}}
   f(d)G_q(ad,\overline\chi)W_{\chi,X}(X/d).
\end{equation}
Restrict first to $d\leqslant L^R$. Lemma~\ref{lem:gauss-pointwise} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:general-weighted-tail} with parameter $B$, together with
\[
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}\frac{\sqrt{(d,q)}}d\leqslant H(q),
\]
show that the characters outside $\mathcal E$ contribute, after division
by $\log X$,
\[
 \ll \frac{X\sqrt q}{\phi(q)}H(q)
       \left(\frac{\log Z_B}{L}\right)^{2/3}
 =o\left(\frac X{\sqrt q}\right).
\]
The terms with $d>L^R$ are $O_A(X/L)$ by
\eqref{eq:general-primary-tail}, since $w_X(n)\leqslant\log X$.

For $\chi\in\mathcal E$ and $Y=X/d$, direct summation of the missing
prime weights gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-remove-weight}
 |(\log X)M_\chi(Y)-W_{\chi,X}(Y)|\ll_A Y\log Z_B.
\end{equation}
Indeed, write $\log X=\log(X/n)+\log n$ and split the prime-power
expansion of $\log n$ at $Z_B$ and $X/Z_B$. Since
$X/L^R\leqslant Y\leqslant X$, the term $\log(X/n)$ has total mass
$O_A(Y\log L)$, and Mertens' theorem bounds each of the two prime ranges
by $O(Y\log Z_B)$; repeated central primes contribute less. Using
\eqref{eq:general-remove-weight} in \eqref{eq:general-weighted-primary}
costs
\[
 \ll \frac X{\sqrt q}\frac q{\phi(q)}H(q)|\mathcal E|
       \frac{\log Z_B}{L}
 =o\left(\frac X{\sqrt q}\right).
\]
Together, \eqref{eq:general-logarithmic-identity}--
\eqref{eq:general-remove-weight} show that only the characters in $\mathcal E$ can contribute significantly to
\eqref{eq:general-primary-exact}.

Take $\mathcal E_q$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:general-level-q-sieve} with parameter $B$. For
$\chi\in\mathcal E\setminus\mathcal E_q$, Cauchy--Schwarz in the
character variable, Lemma~\ref{lem:gauss-pointwise}, and
\eqref{eq:general-level-q-sieve} give, for $d\leqslant L^R$,
\[
 \sum_{\chi\in\mathcal E\setminus\mathcal E_q}
 |G_q(ad,\overline\chi)M_\chi(X/d)|
 \ll \sqrt{q(d,q)}\,|\mathcal E|^{1/2}
      \frac Xd L^{-(1-1/\sqrt2)+o(1)}.
\]
After summing over $d$ and dividing by $\phi(q)$, this is
$o(X/\sqrt q)$. The terms with larger $d\in\mathcal D_q$ are covered by
\eqref{eq:general-kernel-tail}. Hence at most the character in
$\mathcal E_q$ remains, proving \eqref{eq:general-one-character}.

label: lem:general-stability
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:general-relative-complete
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall the completely multiplicative $f^\flat$ and the powerful
convolution $f\mathbf1_{(\cdot,q)=1}=h*f^\flat$ from
\eqref{eq:general-powerful-convolution}.
Apply the Lipschitz theorem
\cite[Theorem~1.5]{GranvilleHarperSoundararajan2019} to
$g(n)=f^\flat(n)\chi(n)\in\mathcal C(1)$.
Let $t$ be its maximizing frequency, with $|t|\leqslant L$.
For each fixed $B>0$, the theorem gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-relative-complete}
 \sum_{n\leqslant x/v}g(n)
 =v^{-1-it}\sum_{n\leqslant x}g(n)
  +O_B\left(\frac{x}{vL^{\eta_2}}\right)
 \qquad(1\leqslant v\leqslant L^B)
\end{equation}
for some absolute $\eta_2>0$.
Indeed, the displayed Lipschitz error is
$L^{-(1-2/\pi)+o(1)}$ for polylogarithmic shortening $v$.

Choose $R$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$ and use
\eqref{eq:general-relative-complete} with $v=uk$ for
$k\leqslant L^R$. Since
$\sum_k|h(k)|/k^{1-\rho}\ll_\rho1$ for $0<\rho<1/2$,
convolution gives
\[
 M_\chi(x/u)=
 u^{-1-it}M_g(x)\sum_{k\geqslant1}
                 \frac{h(k)\chi(k)}{k^{1+it}}
 +O_A\left(\frac{x}{uL^{\eta_1}}\right),
\]
with $\eta_1>0$ after decreasing $\eta_2$.
The tails $k>L^R$ follow from Rankin's trick and the trivial
mean-value bound. Taking $u=1$ in this formula identifies its
main amplitude as $M_\chi(x)$ up to $O(xL^{-\eta_1})$. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-relative-mean}
 M_\chi(x/u)=u^{-1-it}M_\chi(x)
     +O_A\left(\frac{x}{uL^{\eta_1}}\right).
\end{equation}

Write the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:general-stability}
by partial summation in the phase $\mathrm e(\gamma un)$, and use
\eqref{eq:general-relative-mean} at every prefix
$x/L^{B}\leqslant y\leqslant x/u$, with $B$ sufficiently large in terms of $A$.
The omitted smaller prefixes cost $O(x/L^B)$, while
$|\gamma|x\leqslant1$ keeps the integrated error
$O_A(x/(uL^{\eta_1}))$. The main term is
\[
 \frac{M_\chi(x)}{u^{1+it}}
 \left(\mathrm e(\gamma x)-2\pi i\gamma x
  \int_0^1 \mathrm e(\gamma xv)v^{1+it}\,\mathrm{d} v\right)
 =\frac{\mathcal H_x(\gamma,t)}{u^{1+it}}M_\chi(x),
\]
by integration by parts. This proves \eqref{eq:general-stability}.
Finally, take $u=1$. The left side has modulus at most
$\#\{n\leqslant x:(n,q)=1\}=x\phi(q)/q+O(2^{\omega(q)})$,
which gives \eqref{eq:general-amplitude-bound}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $L=\log x$ and first suppose $q\leqslant L^3$. Take $A$ sufficiently
large in Proposition~\ref{prop:general-one-character}. If there is no
exceptional character, the proposition and partial summation in the phase perturbation $\alpha-a/q$ give
$S_f(x,\alpha)=O(x/L)+o(x/\sqrt q)$.

Otherwise let $\chi_0$ be the unique surviving character, and choose
$t$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:general-stability}.
For $x/L^A\leqslant X\leqslant x$ apply the stability lemma to the terms
$d\leqslant L^R$ with $u=xd/X$, enlarging $A$ in terms of the fixed $R$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:general-one-character} and
\eqref{eq:general-kernel-tail} yield uniformly
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-prefix-model}
 S_f(X,a/q)
 =\frac{M_{\chi_0}(x)}{\phi(q)}
   \left(\frac Xx\right)^{1+it}
   \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}
    \frac{f(d)G_q(ad,\overline{\chi_0})}{d^{1+it}}
 +O_A\left(\frac XL\right)+o\left(\frac X{\sqrt q}\right).
\end{equation}
Writing $\alpha=a/q+\beta$, where $|\beta|x\leqslant1/q$,
partial summation in $\mathrm e(\beta n)$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-main-expansion}
\begin{aligned}
 S_f(x,\alpha)
 ={}&\frac{\mathcal H_x(\beta,t)M_{\chi_0}(x)}{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{d\in\mathcal D_q}
 \frac{f(d)G_q(ad,\overline{\chi_0})}{d^{1+it}}\\
 &\quad+O\left(\frac xL\right)+o\left(\frac x{\sqrt q}\right).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The omitted prefixes below $x/L^A$ contribute $O(x/L^A)$.
The uniform errors in \eqref{eq:general-prefix-model} remain of the
same order after partial summation.

Lemma~\ref{lem:general-stability} gives
\[
 |\mathcal H_x(\beta,t)M_{\chi_0}(x)|
 \leqslant\frac{\phi(q)}q x+O\bigl(2^{\omega(q)}+xL^{-\eta_1}\bigr).
\]
The error on the right is $o(x\phi(q)/q)$ for $q\leqslant L^3$.
For general multiplicative $f$, the first estimate in
Lemma~\ref{lem:general-primary-kernel} bounds the kernel in
\eqref{eq:general-main-expansion} by $(4/\sqrt6)\sqrt q$.
This proves \eqref{eq:main-expanded} in the small-modulus range.
If $f$ is completely multiplicative, we instead apply
\eqref{eq:complete-primary-kernel}, obtaining
\eqref{eq:complete-main} from the \emph{same} expansion.

For $L^3<q\leqslant Q_{\rm MV}(x)$ the Montgomery--Vaughan estimate
\eqref{eq:MV-intro}, together with $q/\phi(q)\ll\log\log(3q)$,
gives $S_f(x,a/q)\ll x/L$ for either class of functions.
Lemma~\ref{lem:phase} contributes $O(x/q)$, so the asserted estimates
hold throughout the claimed range.

Finally, the periodic example of
Proposition~\ref{prop:counterexamples}\emph{(i)} attains $4/\sqrt6$,
while primitive characters attain $1$ in the completely multiplicative
class. The error terms are uniform in the stated parameters. Since $q\leqslant x/(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ implies
$q\leqslant Q_{\rm MV}(x)$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and large $x$,
Conjecture~\ref{conj:main} follows.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $L=\log x$. First assume $q\leqslant Q_{\rm MV}(x)$, and set
\[
 U=\max\{x_0,qL^2(\log\log x)^3\},
\]
where $x_0$ is an absolute threshold for Proposition~\ref{prop:basic-bound}.
For $U\leqslant t\leqslant x$, one has $q\leqslant Q_{\rm MV}(t)$ and
$|\alpha-a/q|\leqslant1/(qt)$, so Proposition~\ref{prop:basic-bound} gives
\[
 |S_f(t,\alpha)|\ll\frac{t}{\log t}+\frac{t}{\sqrt q}.
\]
Using $|S_f(t,\alpha)|\leqslant t$ below $U$, partial summation yields
\[
 \left|\sum_{n\leqslant x}\frac{f(n)}n\mathrm e(n\alpha)\right|
 \ll \log U+\log\log x+\frac{L}{\sqrt q}
 \ll \log q+\frac{L}{\sqrt q}.
\]
For the last inequality, note that $\log U\leqslant\log q+O(\log\log x)$, and
$\log\log x\ll\log q+L/\sqrt q$: use $L/\sqrt q\geqslant\log\log x$ if
$q\leqslant(L/\log\log x)^2$, and $\log q\gg\log\log x$ otherwise. If
$Q_{\rm MV}(x)<q\leqslant x$, then $\log q\asymp L$, and the trivial
harmonic bound proves the same assertion. This establishes
\eqref{eq:logarithmic-corollary}.

For the sharp estimates, put $C_0=4/\sqrt6$ in the general case and
$C_0=1$ in the completely multiplicative case. Under the subcritical
hypothesis, choose $T$ by
\[
 \log T=\left(\frac{L\log\log x}{\sqrt q}\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Then $q\leqslant Q_{\rm MV}(T)$ and
\[
 \log T=o(L/\sqrt q),\qquad
 \log\log x=o(L/\sqrt q).
\]
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} therefore implies,
uniformly for $T\leqslant t\leqslant x$,
\[
 |S_f(t,\alpha)|\leqslant(C_0+o(1))\frac{t}{\sqrt q}
          +O\left(\frac{t}{\log t}\right).
\]
The initial segment $n\leqslant T$ contributes $O(\log T)$; partial
summation on $(T,x]$ contributes at most
\[
 (C_0+o(1))\frac{L}{\sqrt q}+O(\log\log x).
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:general-sharp-log} and
\eqref{eq:complete-sharp-log}. For optimality, the periodic construction
in Proposition~\ref{prop:counterexamples}\emph{(i)} gives the
coefficient $4/\sqrt6$ after partial summation; primitive Dirichlet
characters give the coefficient $1$ in the completely multiplicative
case. A direct treatment of the logarithmic sums and further discussion appear in
\cite{GouLogarithmic2026}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\ell\geqslant5$ be a prime, let $\chi$ be a primitive character modulo
$\ell$, and put $q=6\ell$. Define a multiplicative function $g$ by
\[
 g(2^k)=g(3^k)=-1\quad(k\geqslant1),
 \qquad g(p^k)=1\quad(p>3,\ k\geqslant1),
\]
and set $f(n):=g(n)\chi(n)$.  The function $g$ is periodic modulo $6$,
with
\[
 (g(0),g(1),\ldots,g(5))=(1,1,-1,-1,-1,1),
\]
so $f$ is periodic modulo $q$.  Notice that $f$ is multiplicative but
not completely multiplicative.

Write
$\tau(\chi):=\sum_{v\bmod\ell}\chi(v)\mathrm e(v/\ell)$ for the primitive
Gauss sum; then $|\tau(\chi)|=\sqrt\ell$.

Let
\[
 C_q:=\sum_{b\bmod q}f(b)\mathrm e(b/q).
\]
Choose $s$ and $t$ with $s\ell\equiv1\pmod6$ and
$6t\equiv1\pmod\ell$.  The Chinese remainder theorem gives
\[
 C_q=
 \left(\sum_{u\bmod6}g(u)\mathrm e(su/6)\right)
 \left(\sum_{v\bmod\ell}\chi(v)\mathrm e(tv/\ell)\right).
\]
Since $s\equiv\pm1\pmod6$, the first factor equals $4$; the second
equals $\chi(6)\tau(\chi)$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-Cq}
 C_q=4\chi(6)\tau(\chi),\qquad |C_q|=4\sqrt\ell.
\end{equation}
Periodicity now yields
\[
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}f(n)\mathrm e(n/q)
 =\frac{x}{q}C_q+O(q).
\]
Consequently, whenever $q^{3/2}=o(x)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-13}
 \left|\sum_{n\leqslant x}f(n)\mathrm e(n/q)\right|
 =\left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
For example, take primes $\ell_j\to\infty$, put $q_j=6\ell_j$, and
choose $x_j=\exp(q_j)$.  Then $q_j\leqslant(\log x_j)^2$, and
\eqref{eq:counter-13} contradicts the leading constant $1$ in
\cite[(1.3)]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}.  This does not contradict an
order-of-magnitude bound $\ll x/\sqrt q$.

label: eq:counter-average
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $q$ be squarefree, assume $P^+(q)\leqslant y$, and define
\[
 f_q(n):=\mu((n,q)).
\]
This is a periodic, unimodular multiplicative function. For
$a\in(\mathbb{Z}/q\mathbb{Z})^\times$, write
\[
 S_q(a;x,y):=
 \sum_{\substack{n\leqslant x\\P^+(n)\leqslant y}}
 f_q(n)\mathrm e(an/q).
\]
Averaging over the reduced numerators gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-average}
 \frac1{\phi(q)}\sum_{a\bmod q}^{*}S_q(a;x,y)
 =\mu(q)M_q(x,y),
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-Mq}
 M_q(x,y):=\frac1{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{r\mid q}
 \left(\prod_{p\mid r}(p-2)\right)\Psi(x/r,y)>0.
\end{equation}
Indeed, if $d=(n,q)$, then the squarefreeness of $q$ gives
\[
 c_q(n)=\mu(q/d)\phi(d),
 \qquad \mu(d)c_q(n)=\mu(q)\phi(d).
\]
Also
\[
 \phi((n,q))
 =\prod_{p\mid q}\bigl(1+(p-2)\mathbf1_{p\mid n}\bigr).
\]
Expanding the last product and summing over the $y$-smooth integers
gives \eqref{eq:counter-Mq}.  In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-max-a}
 \max_{(a,q)=1}|S_q(a;x,y)|\geqslant M_q(x,y).
\end{equation}
Averaging in \eqref{eq:counter-average} is essential: the corresponding identity need not hold for a fixed numerator $a$.

Choose $x=x(y)$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-saddle-x}
 \log x=\sum_{p\leqslant y}\frac{\log p}{\sqrt p-1}.
\end{equation}
Thus the Hildebrand--Tenenbaum saddle point is $1/2$. Their saddle-point
theorem \cite[Theorems~1 and~3]{HildebrandTenenbaum1986} and its
fixed-dilation consequence give, for each fixed $q$ and each $r\mid q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-local-ratio}
 \frac{\Psi(x/r,y)}{\Psi(x,y)}
 =r^{-1/2}(1+o_q(1))
 \qquad(y\to\infty).
\end{equation}
For completeness, let $\sigma_r$ be the saddle point associated with
$(x/r,y)$. The mean-value theorem in the saddle equation gives
\[
 \sigma_r=\frac12+O_q\!\left(
  \left\{\sum_{p\leqslant y}
  \frac{p^{1/2}(\log p)^2}{(p^{1/2}-1)^2}\right\}^{-1}
 \right)=\frac12+o_q(1).
\]
A Taylor expansion of the two saddle-point formulae, first in the
$\log x$ variable and then in the saddle, therefore gives
$\log\Psi(x/r,y)-\log\Psi(x,y)=-(\log r)/2+o_q(1)$, which is
\eqref{eq:counter-local-ratio}. This is the framework recalled in
\cite[\S3.1]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}; crucially, $q$ is fixed before
$y$ tends to infinity. It follows that
\begin{align}
 M_q(x,y)
 &=(1+o_q(1))\frac{\Psi(x,y)}{\phi(q)}
   \prod_{p\mid q}\left(1+\frac{p-2}{\sqrt p}\right) \notag\\
 &=(1+o_q(1))\frac{\Psi(x,y)}{\sqrt q}\mathfrak A(q),
 \label{eq:counter-Aq-main}
\end{align}
where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-Aq}
 \mathfrak A(q):=
 \prod_{p\mid q}\left(1+\frac1{\sqrt p+1}\right).
\end{equation}
The second equality uses
\[
 \frac{\sqrt p}{p-1}\left(1+\frac{p-2}{\sqrt p}\right)
 =1+\frac1{\sqrt p+1}.
\]

The same saddle-point formula, combined with the prime number theorem,
gives $\log x=(2+o(1))\sqrt y$ and
\[
 \log\left(\frac{\Psi(x,y)\log x}{\sqrt{xy}}\right)
 =\left(2+o(1)\right)\frac{\sqrt y}{\log y}.
\]
Consequently, for every fixed $q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:counter-secondary-small}
 \frac{\sqrt{xy}}{\log x}
 =o\left(\frac{\Psi(x,y)}{\sqrt q}\right).
\end{equation}

Finally take the primorials $q_z:=\prod_{p\leqslant z}p$. The prime number
theorem gives
\begin{align*}
 \log\mathfrak A(q_z)
 &=\sum_{p\leqslant z}\log\left(1+\frac1{\sqrt p+1}\right)\\
 &=\sum_{p\leqslant z}\left(\frac1{\sqrt p}+O\left(\frac1p\right)\right)
 =\left(2+o(1)\right)\frac{\sqrt z}{\log z}\longrightarrow\infty.
\end{align*}
Choose $z_j\to\infty$ and set $q_j=q_{z_j}$.  With $q_j$ fixed,
choose $y_j\geqslant q_j^2$ sufficiently large, define $x_j$ by
\eqref{eq:counter-saddle-x}, and then choose a reduced numerator $a_j$
using \eqref{eq:counter-max-a}.  Equations
\eqref{eq:counter-Aq-main} and \eqref{eq:counter-secondary-small} give
\[
 \frac{|S_{q_j}(a_j;x_j,y_j)|}
 {\Psi(x_j,y_j)/\sqrt{q_j}+\sqrt{x_jy_j}/\log x_j}
 \longrightarrow\infty.
\]
This disproves \cite[(1.4)]{GranvilleLamzouri2026}.  The order of these choices matters: we use the smooth-number asymptotic only with $q$ fixed, without assuming uniformity as $q$ grows.  Since $f_q(p^2)=f_q(p)=-1$ for
$p\mid q$, this example is not completely multiplicative and does not
settle the completely multiplicative version of that problem.

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $q=\lfloor(\log x/\log\log x)^2\rfloor$. For $f\equiv1$ and $\alpha=1/q$,
summation by parts gives
\[
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}\frac{\mathrm e(n/q)}n
 =-\operatorname{Log}(1-\mathrm e(1/q))+O(q/x),
\]
with the principal branch of the logarithm. Hence
\[
 \left|\sum_{n\leqslant x}\frac{\mathrm e(n/q)}n\right|
 =\log q+O(1)=(2+o(1))\log\log x,
\]
whereas $(4/\sqrt6)(\log x)/\sqrt q=(4/\sqrt6+o(1))\log\log x$.
This disproves conjecture~(1.6) at its stated endpoint.
More generally, taking $q\sim c(\log x/\log\log x)^2$ gives the lower leading
coefficient $2\sqrt c$, so the proposed coefficient $4/\sqrt6$ fails
whenever $c>2/3$. See also \cite{GouLogarithmic2026}.

label: prop:critical-counterexample
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:critical-counterexample}
Let $0<c\leqslant1$ be fixed. There exist arbitrarily large $x$, integers
$q$ satisfying
\[
 q=c(\log x)^2,
\]
and $1$-bounded multiplicative functions $f$ such that, with
$\alpha=1/q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:critical-counterexample}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}f(n)\mathrm e(n/q)
 \right|
 \geqslant
 \left(
 \frac4{\sqrt6}+\frac{\sqrt c}{2}+o(1)
 \right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the estimate
\[
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}f(n)\mathrm e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \leqslant
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}
\]
cannot hold uniformly for all $1$-bounded multiplicative $f$ throughout
the range $q\leqslant(\log x)^2$.

name: Counterexample in the critical range

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\ell>3$ tend to infinity through the primes, and take $q=6\ell$ and
\[
 x=\exp\left(\sqrt{\frac q c}\right).
\]
Thus $q=c(\log x)^2$. Let $\chi$ be a non-principal character modulo
$\ell$; since $\ell$ is prime, $\chi$ is primitive.

Define the multiplicative function $g$ on prime powers by
\[
 g(2^k)=g(3^k)=-1\quad(k\geqslant1),
 \qquad
 g(p^k)=1\quad(p>3,\ k\geqslant1).
\]
Then $g$ is periodic modulo $6$, with
\[
 (g(0),g(1),\ldots,g(5))=(1,1,-1,-1,-1,1).
\]
The multiplicative function
\[
 f_0(n)=g(n)\chi(n)
\]
is therefore periodic modulo $q$.

Let $\overline{\ell}$ denote the inverse of $\ell$ modulo $6$, and
$\overline6$ the inverse of $6$ modulo $\ell$. By the Chinese
remainder theorem,
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{b\bmod q}f_0(b)\mathrm e(b/q)
 &=
 \left(
 \sum_{u\bmod6}g(u)\mathrm e(u\overline{\ell}/6)
 \right)
 \left(
 \sum_{v\bmod\ell}\chi(v)\mathrm e(v\overline6/\ell)
 \right).
\end{align*}
Since $\overline{\ell}\equiv\pm1\pmod6$, the first factor is
\[
 1+\mathrm e(1/6)-\mathrm e(1/3)-\mathrm e(1/2)-\mathrm e(2/3)+\mathrm e(5/6)=4,
\]
up to complex conjugation. The second factor is a Gauss sum of absolute
value $\sqrt\ell$. Hence
\[
 \left|
 \sum_{b\bmod q}f_0(b)\mathrm e(b/q)
 \right|
 =4\sqrt\ell.
\]
Using periodicity,
\[
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}f_0(n)\mathrm e(n/q)
 =
 \frac{x}{q}
 \sum_{b\bmod q}f_0(b)\mathrm e(b/q)+O(q),
\]
and consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:f0-major}
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}f_0(n)\mathrm e(n/q)
 \right|
 =
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q},
\end{equation}
since $q^{3/2}=o(x)$.

We next show that primes in $(x/2,x]$ make a negligible contribution to
\eqref{eq:f0-major}. For such primes $p$ one has $g(p)=1$, and hence
\[
 \sum_{x/2<p\leqslant x}f_0(p)\mathrm e(p/q)
 =
 \sum_{x/2<p\leqslant x}\chi(p)\mathrm e(p/q).
\]
Since $q\ll(\log x)^2$, the Siegel--Walfisz theorem, applied after
splitting the primes into residue classes modulo $q$, gives
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{x/2<p\leqslant x}\chi(p)\mathrm e(p/q)
 &=
 \frac{Li(x)-Li(x/2)}{\phi(q)}
 \sum_{\substack{b\bmod q\\(b,q)=1}}
 \chi(b)\mathrm e(b/q)
 +O_A\left(\frac{x}{(\log x)^A}\right)
\end{align*}
for every fixed $A>0$.

The finite sum again factors by the Chinese remainder theorem:
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{\substack{b\bmod q\\(b,q)=1}}
 \chi(b)\mathrm e(b/q)
 &=
 \left(
 \sum_{u\in(\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z})^\times}
 \mathrm e(u\overline{\ell}/6)
 \right)
 \left(
 \sum_{v\bmod\ell}\chi(v)\mathrm e(v\overline6/\ell)
 \right).
\end{align*}
The first factor has absolute value $1$, while the second has absolute
value $\sqrt\ell$. Since $\phi(q)=2(\ell-1)$, it follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large-primes-f0}
 \sum_{x/2<p\leqslant x}f_0(p)\mathrm e(p/q)
 =
 o\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt q}\right).
\end{equation}

Consequently, if
\[
 S_*=
 \sum_{\substack{n\leqslant x\\
 n\notin\{p:x/2<p\leqslant x\}}}
 f_0(n)\mathrm e(n/q),
\]
then \eqref{eq:f0-major} and \eqref{eq:large-primes-f0} imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Sstar}
 |S_*|
 =
 \left(\frac4{\sqrt6}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\end{equation}
For sufficiently large $x$ this is non-zero; write
$S_*=\omega|S_*|$ with $|\omega|=1$.

We now modify $f_0$ only at primes $p\in(x/2,x]$. Define a
multiplicative function $f$ on prime powers by
\[
 f(p)=\omega\mathrm e(-p/q),
 \qquad
 f(p^k)=f(p)^k
 \quad
 \left(\frac x2<p\leqslant x,\ k\geqslant2\right),
\]
and retain
\[
 f(p^k)=f_0(p^k)
\]
at every other prime power. This defines a $1$-bounded multiplicative
function.

If $p>x/2$, then $2p>x$ and $p^2>x$. Thus, among the integers
$n\leqslant x$, changing the value at such a prime affects only the term
$n=p$. Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}f(n)\mathrm e(n/q)
 &=
 S_*+
 \sum_{x/2<p\leqslant x}f(p)\mathrm e(p/q)\\
 &=
 \omega\left(
 |S_*|+\pi(x)-\pi(x/2)
 \right).
\end{align*}
By the prime number theorem,
\[
 \pi(x)-\pi(x/2)
 =
 \left(\frac12+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\log x}
 =
 \left(\frac{\sqrt c}{2}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:Sstar} proves
\eqref{eq:critical-counterexample}.

label: rem:critical-counterexample
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:critical-counterexample}
The construction exhibits two independent sources of large values.
The first comes from the Gauss sums at the primes $2$ and
$3$, which contribute
\[
 \frac4{\sqrt6}\frac{x}{\sqrt q}.
\]
The second comes from the unrestricted values of a multiplicative
function at primes $p>x/2$, and contributes
\[
 \left(\frac12+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\log x}.
\]
At the critical scale $q\sim c(\log x)^2$ these two quantities have the
same order of magnitude and can be arranged to have the same phase.
Thus any sharp critical-scale estimate of the form
\[
 \left|
 \sum_{n\leqslant x}f(n)\mathrm e(n\alpha)
 \right|
 \leqslant
 \bigl(C(c)+o(1)\bigr)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}
\]
must satisfy
\[
 C(c)\geqslant\frac4{\sqrt6}+\frac{\sqrt c}{2}.
\]
In particular, at the endpoint $q\sim(\log x)^2$ one necessarily has
\[
 C(1)\geqslant\frac4{\sqrt6}+\frac12.
\]
The large-prime contribution is $o(x/\sqrt q)$ when
$q=o((\log x)^2)$, in agreement with
Corollary~\ref{cor:sharp-range}.

A similar construction shows that the range in Corollary~\ref{cor:sharp-range} is also optimal for completely multiplicative functions. Take $q$ prime and use a
primitive character modulo $q$ as the initial completely multiplicative
function. Modifying its values at primes in $(x/2,x]$ and then extending
completely multiplicatively gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{n\leqslant x}f(n)\mathrm e(n/q)\right|
 \geqslant\left(1+\frac{\sqrt c}{2}+o(1)\right)\frac{x}{\sqrt q}
\]
when $q\sim c(\log x)^2$.
